claim: Playing out an interaction between role-holders forecasts real conflict decisions about twice as accurately as game-theorist or unaided judgement (62% vs 31% over 8 conflicts in Green 2005; 61% vs 28% over 5 interactive situations in Armstrong's audit of the earlier 6-situation study). Both rest on one research programme, so independence is partial. Gap search: no outside-lab replication and no LLM-role-player test found (search incomplete); status lowered to single-source programme.
agent_test: On tasks with a known counter-actor outcome, compare one-shot adversary prediction vs a separate-call adversary that plays the reply, at equal total tokens, scored by code against the known outcome.

claim: The role-play advantage depends on interaction between parties: in the one non-interactive situation (Panalba) game theory beat role playing, so a wargame step is warranted only when a reacting party exists.
agent_test: Run the test step on tasks with and without a counter-actor; check that skipping it on no-adversary tasks saves tokens with no accuracy loss.

claim: Combining several independent role-play runs gave an accurate forecast in 7 of 8 conflicts (single-run accuracy 62%); the modal game-theorist forecast was right in only 3 of 8.
agent_test: Run the adversary role N times (N=1,3,5) at equal total tokens and compare single vs code-aggregated modal reply.

claim: A model-played opponent is a high-variance sample: free-form advice from all five tested LMs on one crisis prompt differs in meaning; inconsistency stays above rewording noise at T>0.2, and meaning-preserving rewrites give inconsistency about equal to sampling at T=0.2 (GPT-4 is the exception, lower under rewrites).
agent_test: Run the adversary 5 times on 3 paraphrases of the brief; measure the share of runs that name the same top weakness (code-extracted).

claim: Same-model-on-all-sides LLM crisis simulations escalate: all five models in Rivera et al. showed significant initial escalation and none de-escalated significantly in any of 3 scenarios; the untuned base model was most severe. Partly replicated in direction by Elbaum and Panter with a 7B model (baseline escalation nonzero, depends on sampling).
agent_test: Compare plan weaknesses found by a same-model opponent vs a differently briefed or different-model opponent against seeded known flaws.

claim: The simulated opponent's aggressiveness is a dial set by prompt and sampling: lowering temperature from 1.0 to 0.01 cut mean escalation 48% and a de-escalation reflection prompt cut it 57% in a 7B model (10 runs per cell); in Rivera, GPT-3.5 No-Goals and Low-Stakes prompts also cut severe actions significantly. A red team measures the brief as much as the plan.
agent_test: Run the same plan against adversary briefs of varied stance at fixed temperature; check that the weaknesses found are stable across stances.
audit: downgraded 2026-10-27 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Persona labels do not move simulated players: telling LLM teams that all players were pacifists or sociopaths changed no action significantly, and varying background distributions had no effect (GPT-3.5, GPT-4, GPT-4o).
agent_test: Compare persona-labelled adversary variants vs variants that differ in rules or information; count distinct code-verified weaknesses at equal tokens.

claim: Simulated team dialogue inside one model is near-unanimous (authors call it farcical harmony), and dialogue length changed aggressiveness and action counts in ways that did not match humans; it does not supply real objection.
agent_test: Compare an in-call debate vs a separate-call adversary with its own brief: share of runs with a code-verified distinct objection.

claim: LLM wargame teams reproduce the direction of human treatment effects but not exact choices: with 214 experts in 48 teams, LLM action frequency matched humans on 16/21 (GPT-3.5), 10/21 (GPT-4) and 9/21 (GPT-4o) actions; newer models matched fewer. Single scenario. 2026 side evidence: six 2026 models matched graduate-student choices in 4 menu simulations at 0.25-0.54 in round 1 and 0.16-0.33 in round 2 (n = 63 and 45).
agent_test: Use the test step for a sensitivity sweep over assumptions and check rank agreement with ground-truth ablations.

claim: Current models are far below humans at opponent modelling and complex situation analysis in one wargame benchmark (opponent modelling: best LLM 49.1 vs general-level humans 77.9; complex situation analysis 37.5% vs 85.9%), with the biggest gaps on short-term and high-risk adversary behaviour. Scoring of policy generation uses an LLM judge.
agent_test: Compare giving the adversary a code-built goal and option list vs asking the model to infer intent, at equal tokens.

claim: Models predict long-horizon reward well (R1 84.0 vs human 83.3) but short-term moves poorly (45.2 vs human 87.8); plan quality is reported to degrade with plan length and at mid-game pivots.
agent_test: Test a plan as short rollout steps with code-held state vs one long imagined campaign at equal tokens.

claim: Almost no AI-wargame work lets the model both act and adjudicate: 20 of 223 studies (9%), 4 of 63 core military studies. LLM adjudication is the least tested and hardest part. The coding is single-coder with LM help. Gap search: the only measured study found (Epstein 2026, 378 actions, 9 games) tests self-consistency, not accuracy: judge re-runs changed 3-6% of outcomes under bounded adjustment and 14-16% under free judgement; a claimed kappa of 0.89 against humans came from a withdrawn paper and is not usable.
agent_test: Compare LLM adjudication vs code-rule adjudication on tasks with known rule outcomes: agreement rate and invented-consequence rate.

claim: Review and position sources name the same hazards of LLM wargames (role collapse, adjudication opacity, escalation-through-adjudication, unfaithful reasoning, prompt sensitivity). Riedl and Matlin argue these; they do not measure them.
agent_test: Measure role collapse: correlation of errors across planner, adversary and judge calls when one model fills all three vs different models.

claim: Simulated history can look accurate through memory: WarAgent WWI reproduced key alliances and Austria-Serbia, Austria-Russia and Germany-Russia declarations in 100% of 7 runs, but Britain-Germany war in only 14.3%; fit to known history is weak evidence of predictive power. Gap search: general evidence supports the worry (effective cutoffs precede stated ones by up to 8 months; prompt hints leave leakage; retrieval adds it), but no anonymised or post-cutoff test of a wargame simulation was found.
agent_test: Run the wargame step on anonymised or post-cutoff scenarios vs well-known ones and compare accuracy.

claim: A different kind of opponent finds holes a same-type prompted LLM misses: an RL no-press policy exploited prompted LLM agents far more effectively than prompted LLM exploiters did (one run per exploiter set). Gap search: in IFPV, a prompted LLM opponent (GLM-5) exposed fewer flaws than a scripted one on the same plans (suppression 0-33% vs 35-93%), while a world-model opponent exposed the most.
agent_test: Compare weaknesses found by a code-search adversary (enumerate options) vs a prompted-LLM adversary on seeded-flaw plans.

claim: Courses of action proposed by an LLM and scored by running them in a simulator came within 3.4% of a human expert after human feedback (5 COAs x 10 simulations), far cheaper than RL; the enemy was scripted and RL numbers were copied from earlier papers.
agent_test: Generate plans, score each by code rollout, and compare to model-opinion ranking at equal tokens.

claim: Reflective memory plus opponent modelling plus self-play improved Diplomacy play without human data: win 6.83% vs 6.03% against Cicero (small gap, no significance test), and win 9.10% vs 1.63%, defeated 34.30% vs 61.37% against AutoGPT agents.
agent_test: Store lessons from past simulated runs that held up under checks and measure gains on later similar tasks at equal tokens.

claim: Wargaming as a method has no outcome-level evidence that it improves real plans: the 1870 Prussian success is one confounded case, rigid-vs-free Kriegsspiel was settled by officer preference, validation against hypothetical futures is hard, and no controlled test of an LLM plan improving after a wargame step was found. Gap search: case evidence exists (Millennium Challenge 2002 red team sank 19 ships and was then constrained until the end state was scripted per the JFCOM report; 1933 Navy game found logistics and repair problems) but only from secondary sources, and IFPV (2026) shows a simulator gain with unequal compute.
schema_part: G7 (test value on our own tasks)
agent_test: A/B on tasks with seeded flaws: plan with vs without the wargame step at equal tokens, scored by flaw recall and false alarms.
audit_note: Kriegsspiel page (Prussia only army wargaming, Meckel/Verdy du Vernois), Zenko (19 ships, $250M, 752-page report, end state scripted) and IFPV (+19.4% relative gain in a different setup than Table 3) verified; 'unequal compute' is an inference since the paper reports no compute figures; negative 'no controlled test found' not checkable.

claim: The statement that computer-run wargames escalate to nuclear use more than human-played ones is passed on by two LLM papers (Emery 2021; Brewer and Blair 1979). Emery 2021 as read compares one abstract MAD game (nuclear use) with one realistic human-played game (none) and blames abstraction and missing felt responsibility; it does not show a general computer effect. Brewer and Blair 1979 was not found.
agent_test: Do not rely on it. Treat as a hypothesis: model-run opponents lack stakes.

claim: Feeding the adversary's concrete counter-move into the prompt lowered response inconsistency for most models.
schema_part: O (work backwards from a stated reply)
agent_test: Compare an open-ended adversary vs an adversary given a code-built list of candidate counter-moves: run-to-run agreement and weakness yield.

claim: Wargame designs separate umpire from players (Kriegsspiel umpire, Snow Globe control agent, WarAgent secretary checker): rules or code count and validate, judgment supplies plausible consequences. This is design practice shared across sources, not an outcome result.
agent_test: Ablate the separate validator on opponent moves: rate of illegal or invented moves entering state, with and without.
audit_note: Kriegsspiel page (Reisswitz umpire, dice, 1:8000 maps, Meckel/Verdy du Vernois), Snow Globe (control adjudicates, adjudication hardest, 'Include unexpected consequences' with Mistral-7B-OpenOrca) and WarAgent (secretary agent verifies actions, up to 4 exchanges) verified; Kriegsspiel two listings are one Wikipedia page.

claim: Adjudication stability depends on how much freedom the LLM umpire gets. Same judge on re-run changed 3-6% of outcomes when it could only adjust a rulebook number and 14-16% when it set difficulty alone; four-judge panel changed 40 of 378 outcomes but the pass count by only 8. Aggregate pass rates hide ruling-level change. Accuracy against humans was not measured.
agent_test: Re-run the adjudicator step twice on the same moves; log the share of changed verdicts; compare bounded-adjustment against free judgement.

claim: A prompted LLM opponent can be a weaker plan tester than a simple scripted one, and a world-model opponent can be stronger than both: on the same candidate plans, suppression was GLM-5 0-33%, scripted 35-93%, world-model 47-98% in a combat simulator.
agent_test: Run three adversaries (same-model persona, different model, code enumerator) on the same seeded-flaw plans and compare flaw recall.

claim: One adversary response overstates plan strength; the first few sampled responses carry most of the drop. In a synthetic COA benchmark, BLUE advantage fell .516, .498, .490, .485, .479 for 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 RED samples and win rate fell .920 to .820. Strategic-game model comparisons needed about 150 seeds to stabilise.
agent_test: Measure flaw-set overlap between 1, 3, 5 and 10 adversary runs on the same plan and stop when new flaws per run drop to near zero.

claim: In Payne's 21 model-vs-model nuclear-crisis games no model ever chose accommodation or surrender (only de-escalation as far as returning to the start line) and strategic-threat level was reached in 29-64% of games depending on the model; in Solopova et al.'s menu simulations models' explanations were cooperative in framing but their actions were mixed against graduate-student players (some more coercive); one-line framing moved escalation from 10.7% to 28.6% in 3,604 games (Adl and Williams). No Lamparth replication with experts was found.
agent_test: Fix the adversary frame and model per run, log them, and compare findings across two frames.
audit_note: Payne (21 games, 29-64%) and Adl & Williams (3,604 games, 10.7% to 28.6%) verified, but Solopova et al. does not show models pick more cooperative actions than graduate students (only their explanations are cooperative in framing; some models were more coercive on economic choices), and Payne's models did sometimes reduce violence (return to start line) though never chose accommodation or withdrawal.
claim_before_audit: 2026 models still escalate in model-vs-model play (no model chose a de-escalating option in 21 games; strategic-threat level reached in 29-64% of games) yet pick more cooperative actions than graduate-student players in menu simulations, and one-line framing moved escalation from 10.7% to 28.6% in 3,604 games. Adversary tone is set by task structure and frame, not by model alone. No Lamparth replication with experts was found.

claim: The adversarial plan-verification step has only simulator evidence: IFPV raised mission success to 61.0% vs 49.3% for the best single-step LLM planner under the same world-model test, but success was scored by the same adversary used in design and compute was not matched. At equal compute on reasoning QA, debate and mixture-of-agents beat self-consistency by 1.3 and 2.7 points.
agent_test: Seeded-flaw A/B at equal tokens: plan alone, plan plus self-critique, plan plus separate-call adversary; score by code for flaw recall and false alarms.

claim: The Millennium Challenge 2002 record shows a red team finding a real weakness (blue relied on familiar tactics; 19 ships lost in minutes by one account) and the control cell then constraining red until the end state was scripted, per the exercise report. The finding was documented but initially not acted on. Source is secondary.
schema_part: G5 (adversary findings not edited by planner)
agent_test: Log every override of an adversary finding with its reason and count how often overrides were later wrong.
